newsitem.title: INDIA: FUND VIEW-Stable Indian stocks lure foreign money.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW-Stable Indian stocks lure foreign money.

text.p: India's relatively stable stock market offers a safer bet to foreign money as some other Asian markets are more vulnerable to inflation worries and changes in U.S. interest rates, fund managers and brokers said.
The best thing going India's way was growth potential and its ability to offset Wall Street's movements and the impact on stocks around the world, they said.

"There's negative co-relation to the U.S. and other markets because foreign exposures are limited in India," said Gul Tekchandani, chief investment officer at Sun Foreign and Colonial Asset Management Company.

Only foreign institutional investors are allowed to buy stocks in India, and since the country opened up its markets in 1993, the net inflows from such investors have totalled just $7 billion -- about one-third of the annual inflows that smaller countries like Malaysia or Indonesia get.

But Indian stocks are now slowly emerging from a two-year slide, boosted by a pro-business government budget for the fiscal year beginning on April 1 which cut corporate and personal taxes and raised foreign portfolio holding limits in Indian firms.
"We have a good story to tell," said Anand Rathi, a newly elected director at the 127-year old Bombay Stock Exchange, one of Asia's oldest. "India looks irresistible after the budget."
Net foreign institutional investor inflow in calendar 1997 is expected to range from $3 billion to $4.5 billion compared with about $3 billion in 1996, analysts said.
Rathi believes foreign funds should look more seriously at India because it provided a safety net against rate hikes in the U.S., which often unsettle other Asian markets.
"The political and economic risk in India is limited," he said. "We have a stable administration and continuity of policies."
India's 15-party coalition government, comprising communist and left-leaning parties, have continued to spur economic reform with a focus on wider acceptance of freer markets.
"The key to luring foreign money is good valuations," said Bharat Shah, chief investment officer at Birla Capital International. "It's not the spill-over demand."
He has put money into high-growth software stocks, cash-rich personal care firms and the non-cyclical pharmaceuticals backed by multinational brands.

Shares of internationally competitive automobile components firms were good buys, he said, as the automobile sector's low base promises scope for growth. Some cement and engineering stocks were also attractive.
But the steel sector was seen as taboo.
"It's a cash guzzling business. I find no company that's internationally competitive," he said.
Sun's Tekchandani said infrastructure stocks, telephone and banking shares represented good buys.
